entries.what_happened: One manuscript in the family: “A power saving for planar halving lines” (OpenAI, dated September 25, 2026). Its Theorem 1 (thm:halving-power) says there are absolute constants ε>0, C and n0 such that every even n ≥ n0 and every n-point set in R² with no three collinear has h(P) ≤ C n^{4/3−ε} unordered halving pairs; since distinct pairs give distinct lines, this bounds halving lines too. This improves the classical O(n^{4/3}) halving-line bound that the introduction attributes to Dey (1998). The core is Theorem 2 (thm:all-ranks): for a generic N-point planar configuration and any rank k, the number of switches S_k(P) in a rank-k sweep is at most C N^{4/3−ε}, uniformly in k. The middle-rank case gives Theorem 1. Corollary 3 (cor:k-sensitive) is the k-set statement: for every n-point Q ⊂ R² with no three collinear and every 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2, the number of k-sets is at most C₀ n (k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}, with absolute ε₀ > 0 (the proof takes ε₀ = min{ε, 1/6}). The same bound is given for the complexity of a level in an arrangement of n non-vertical lines with no parallel pair and no three concurrent. Dey's bound for k-sets is O(n(k+1)^{1/3}) (stated in the manuscript's introduction), so the new result improves the exponent of (k+1) from 1/3 to 1/3−ε₀. At k near n/2 it gives about n^{4/3−ε₀}, the same order as the new halving bound. The proof is a finite reduction to exchange graphs and crossing counts, followed by a proof by contradiction that produces a uniform little-o improvement of a packing estimate. That improvement is taken from a limiting spatial measure of dimension 32/17, and a fixed-scale induction turns it into the power saving. The manuscript gives no lower-bound result of its own. It recalls the existing lower bounds for halving lines, Ω(n log n) from Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus and n·exp(Ω(√log n)) from Tóth and Nivasch, and says they remain far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}.
entries.delivers: For the upper-bound half of the problem, the claim establishes: (i) for planar halving lines, a bound of O(n^{4/3−ε}) for even n ≥ n0 with no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε > 0; (ii) for planar k-sets, a bound of O(n(k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}) for all 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2 and no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε₀ > 0; (iii) the same level-complexity bound for arrangements of complete straight lines (not pseudolines, not segments), which the manuscript says gives no corresponding saving for pseudolines or line segments. The constants and exponents are nonquantitative: no numerical value of ε, ε₀, C, C₀ or n0 is given. The results are planar only. Nothing in the manuscript is stated for dimensions above two. The claim is an upper bound only. It gives no lower bound for k-sets or for halving lines, and it does not show that the upper and lower bounds have the same order. The abstract and the theorems describe a power saving over O(n^{4/3}); the manuscripts do not claim to settle the problem, and their framing does not say the problem is solved.
entries.remains: If the claim is correct, the following remain open. (a) Halving lines: the gap between the new upper bound n^{4/3−ε} and the known lower bounds of order n·exp(Ω(√log n)) (and the older Ω(n log n)) is not closed, and the manuscript itself says the lower bounds stay far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}. (b) K-sets: the manuscripts give no lower bound at all for the maximum number of k-sets as a function of n and k, so the matching-bounds question for part (a) of problem_asks is open in full. The k-dependence exponent 1/3−ε₀ is not claimed to be tight. (c) The value of the exponent is not determined, so even the upper bound is not explicit. (d) Dimensions above two, and pseudoline or segment settings, are not addressed.
entries.direction: improves an upper bound: a power saving over O(n^{4/3}) for planar halving lines, and an improved exponent in (k+1) for planar k-sets; no lower bound
entries.conditional_on: No unproven hypothesis is assumed by the theorems. Some steps rely on cited external results that the manuscript does not reprove: the shallow-cutting lemma of Matoušek as stated by Agarwal, Aronov, Chan and Sharir (used for the level and k-set corollary, in recurrence.tex, where the cut-to-level step is stated as following from the cited reduction); and standard background cited in the introduction (Simon 2014 for differentiation of finite measures; Chabrillac and Crouzeix 1987 for monotone-function differentiability, which the text also proves in outline). The imbalanced crossing argument is attributed to Pach, Solymosi and Tardos, and the classical crossing lemma to Ajtai et al. and Leighton; the manuscript says it reproves the reduction and constants it needs. The chain-partition mechanism is stated to be the one underlying Dey (1998). No other OpenAI manuscript is cited or used.
entries.doubts: (1) The power saving depends on Theorem activity-packing, a little-o improvement of a packing estimate. Its proof is by contradiction (rank-limits.tex opens with 'suppose, for a contradiction'; boundary.tex closes it) and runs through rank coordinates, differentiability, a zoom lemma, a spatial measure, and a strip count. That chain is long and several links are stated in prose. The introduction says the conditional-measure and Lipschitz-differentiability statements are 'specified at their applications'. (2) The introduction calls the limit order 'crucial': limits are taken first at a fixed small rank scale and then far along the sequence of configurations. boundary.tex also says that restriction to G is done only after weak convergence, and that the limits along countably many windows come from diagonal subsequences. (3) finite.tex, eq. (finite-localized-crossing), keeps an additive 13824 S³ term, and the text says this term 'may only be discarded after an appropriate limiting normalization'. (4) Some proofs are only partly written out. The spatial proposition's proof begins with 'We first select a positive set' and relies on a metric input stated only as eq. (spatial-metric-input), with its own quantifiers. The zoom lemma is called elementary but its proof is long. (5) The k-set corollary's level-to-cell step is given in outline ('the cited shallow-cutting reduction now gives'). (6) The abstract, the introduction and Theorem 1 agree with each other. I found no inconsistency between the statements and the main theorems. The text says the constants are nonquantitative, which limits how far the bound can be checked numerically.
